title: Html semantics — Module Quiz
description: Mixed quiz covering all topics in Html semantics.

questions.question: Which of these is a SEMANTIC element (conveys meaning), not just a generic container?
questions.explanation:
describes self-contained content.
/ are generic and carry no meaning;
is a line break.

questions.question: How many <main> elements should a single HTML document contain?

options.text: None is required, but max three

questions.explanation: There must be exactly ONE <main> per document — it represents the dominant unique content. Multiple <main> elements break assistive-tech expectations.

questions.question: What implicit ARIA role does the <nav> element expose to assistive technology?
questions.explanation: Browsers map <nav> to role="navigation". <header>→banner, <footer>→contentinfo, <section>→region.

questions.question: Which element should wrap an independent, reusable piece of content (e.g. a blog post or comment)?
questions.explanation: <article> marks content that is independently distributable (posts, comments, cards). <section> groups thematically related content; <aside> is tangential.

questions.question: Why does semantic HTML help SEO?

options.text: It makes the page load faster
Search crawlers infer structure/meaning and rank content better
It removes the need for meta tags

questions.explanation: Crawlers use semantics to understand hierarchy and topic relevance, improving indexing/ranking. It is not a direct speed or font effect.

questions.question: A common mistake is using <section> purely for styling. What is the correct rule?

options.text: Use <section> only when it has a heading and groups related content
Use <section> for every box you want to style
Nest as many <main> as needed inside <section>

questions.explanation: A section should group thematically related content, typically with a heading. For pure styling use <div>. Never nest multiple <main>.

questions.question: What does the <time> element with a datetime attribute provide?

options.text: A live clock on the page
Machine-readable date/time for parsers and search engines

questions.explanation: <time datetime="..."> gives parsers/search engines a standardized value (e.g. 2025-01-01T09:00Z) while showing human text inside.

questions.question: In Angular templates, why is using semantic tags (article/header/footer) recommended?

options.text: It produces accessible, well-structured component layouts
It is required by Angular CLI
It removes the need for RxJS

questions.explanation: Semantic tags in component templates give accessible, maintainable structure — a frontend best practice, not an Angular requirement.

questions.question: What does a11y stand for and what problem does it solve?

options.text: Accessibility; making digital experiences usable by people with disabilities

questions.explanation: a11y = accessibility (a + 11 letters + y). It ensures people with visual/auditory/motor/cognitive impairments can use the product.

questions.question: Which is the BEST practice when building a custom clickable component?

options.text: Use <div role="button" tabindex="0"> and re-implement keyboard handling
Use <span onclick> with no keyboard support

questions.explanation: Native <button> gives focus, keyboard (Enter/Space), and role for free. ARIA should only be added when native elements can't be used (first rule of ARIA).

questions.question: An image used purely for decoration should be made invisible to screen readers by:
questions.explanation: Empty alt="" tells assistive tech to ignore the image. Descriptive alt is for meaningful images; missing alt is an a11y failure.

questions.question: What does the 'first rule of ARIA' state?

options.text: Always use role attributes on every element
Use native HTML elements with built-in semantics before reaching for ARIA
ARIA overrides everything, so use it liberally

questions.explanation: First rule: if a native element or attribute has the semantics you need, use it instead of ARIA, which can override and break native behavior.

questions.question: Which Angular CDK utility announces dynamic changes to screen-reader users?
questions.explanation: LiveAnnouncer (from @angular/cdk/a11y) pushes text to an aria-live region so SR users hear updates like 'Item added to cart'.

questions.question: A modal dialog must trap focus. Why?

options.text: To prevent the user from scrolling the background
So keyboard users cannot escape into background content while the dialog is open

questions.explanation: Focus trapping keeps keyboard/Tab navigation inside the modal so users don't lose context in background content — a core a11y requirement.

questions.question: Which is a common accessibility mistake?

options.text: Missing alt text on informative images

questions.explanation: Missing alt text, poor contrast, and non-keyboard-operable controls are the classic a11y failures to avoid.

questions.question: What do browser accessibility APIs (AXAPI/UIA/AT-SPI) do?

options.text: Expose accessible names/states from the DOM to assistive technologies

questions.explanation: The accessibility tree (built from DOM + ARIA) is exposed via platform APIs so screen readers can announce names, roles, and states.

questions.question: What does ARIA stand for and what does it provide?

options.text: Accessible Rich Internet Applications; roles/states/properties for accessibility

questions.explanation: ARIA = Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It adds role, aria-* state, and property attributes for widgets native HTML can't express.

questions.question: Which attribute would you use to tell a screen reader the CURRENT value of a custom slider (min 0, max 100, now 50)?
questions.explanation: For role="slider" you expose aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax so SRs announce the live value range.

questions.question: What does aria-live="polite" do?

options.text: Announces dynamic content changes to SR users without interrupting current speech

questions.explanation: aria-live regions announce updates. 'polite' queues after current speech; 'assertive' interrupts. Essential for toasts/status updates.

questions.question: A key pitfall: <div role="button"> is NOT clickable by itself. Why?

options.text: Because role adds full functionality automatically
Because role only changes the accessibility tree; you must add JS for click + keyboard (Enter/Space)
Because it requires a form wrapper

questions.explanation: ARIA role is semantic only — it does not add behavior. A <button> gives click + Enter/Space for free; a div needs manual JS.

questions.question: When should you AVOID using ARIA?

options.text: On every element to be safe
When a native HTML element already provides the needed semantics
Never; ARIA is always better than HTML

questions.explanation: First rule of ARIA: prefer native HTML. Adding ARIA can override and break native semantics if done incorrectly.

questions.question: In a tab interface, which ARIA pattern is correct for the selected tab?
questions.explanation: Tabs use role="tab" with aria-selected (true/false) and aria-controls pointing to the associated tabpanel — follows WAI-ARIA APG.

questions.question: What is aria-hidden="true" used for?

options.text: To hide content visually from all users
To remove an element from the accessibility tree (SR ignores it) while still showing it visually
To delete the element from DOM

questions.explanation: aria-hidden removes a node from the a11y tree (e.g. decorative icons) but keeps it visible. Never put aria-hidden on focusable content.

questions.question: Which Angular library relies heavily on ARIA patterns for keyboard nav & screen readers?
questions.explanation: Angular Material components (Menu, Dialog, Tabs, CDK Overlay) implement WAI-ARIA patterns for accessibility out of the box.

questions.question: SEO stands for:
questions.explanation: SEO improves a site's visibility in organic (non-paid) search results via content, technical, and authority signals.

questions.question: The three core stages a search engine follows are:
questions.explanation: Bots crawl URLs, index parsed content, then rank pages by relevance/authority for a query.

questions.question: A <link rel='canonical'> tells search engines:

options.text: Which URL is the preferred/authoritative version of duplicate content

questions.explanation: Canonical URLs consolidate ranking signals and avoid duplicate-content penalties across near-identical pages.

questions.question: Structured data (schema.org JSON-LD) is used to:

options.text: Help search engines understand content and enable rich results (snippets)

questions.explanation: Schema markup lets Google show rich results (ratings, FAQs). JSON-LD is the recommended format.

questions.question: For SPAs (like Angular), the main SEO challenge is:

options.text: Content is rendered client-side, so crawlers may not see it without SSR/prerendering

questions.explanation: Client-rendered HTML can be empty when crawled; SSR (Angular Universal) or prerendering fixes crawlability.

questions.question: Keyword stuffing is harmful because it:

options.text: Reads unnaturally and can trigger search-engine spam penalties

questions.explanation: Overusing keywords looks spammy; modern algorithms reward natural, relevant content over density.
